cards.text: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, is writing a letter to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion. He just told them God chose to give us birth through the word of truth. Now he says, "My beloved brothers, understand this:"

cards.question: James gives his beloved brothers three things to watch. Which one should everyone be QUICK to do?
James also says everyone should be slow to speak and slow to anger.

cards.text: Slow to anger, huh? Baker, I once yelled at my oven for taking too long to preheat, and that oven preheated at the EXACT. SAME. SPEED.

cards.question: James gives a reason to be slow to anger. What is it?

answers.text: It doesn't bring about the righteousness God desires
It makes the people around you stop listening
It shows you don't have enough faith in God

cards.text: So James says to clean house. Get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, like emptying out a junk drawer, and trust me, friend, I KNOW junk drawers.

cards.question: Once the evil is cleared out, James says to humbly accept something. What is it?
James says the word planted in them can save their souls.
James says hearing the word isn't enough on its own. What else should his brothers be?
James says if you only hear the word and stop there, you're deceiving ___.

cards.text: Then James paints a picture. Someone who hears the word but doesn't carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror.

cards.question: After the man in the mirror looks himself over, he walks away and remembers exactly what he looks like.

cards.text: He forgets his own FACE. That's like opening the oven, seeing the batch burning, shutting the door and walking off whistling.

cards.question: But James says there's another kind of person, who looks intently into something and keeps at it. What does he look into?

answers.text: The record of his own deeds

cards.question: James says that person, not a forgetful hearer but an effective doer, will be blessed in what he hears.

cards.text: Then James says someone can think he's religious and still not bridle his tongue. Baker, I talk in ALL CAPS half the time, so this verse is looking RIGHT at me.

cards.question: That man deceives his heart. And James says his religion is ___.

cards.text: Then James shows what religion that's pure and undefiled before our God and Father looks like. It comes in two parts.

cards.question: James says pure religion means caring for ___ and ___ in their distress.
James says the other part of pure religion is keeping yourself from being polluted by the world.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke. It tells no new part of the passage. It repeats 'slow to anger' from verse 19, which cards 2 and 3 already covered, and doesn't move the baker forward.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: The card stacks two comparisons on the same fact: 'clean house' and 'like emptying out a junk drawer.' The junk drawer image also presents the drawer's contents, which in his backstory are his friends, as 'moral filth.' That clashes with his kindness toward them.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: 'Once the evil is cleared out' adds an order the text doesn't give. James 1:21 gives two commands side by side: get rid of filth, and humbly accept the word. It never says one comes after the other.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The core action in James 1:24 is seeing yourself and then immediately forgetting. The comparison shows someone seeing a burning batch and choosing to ignore it, which is ignoring, not forgetting. The card's first line also only restates the answer to card 12.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Bridling the tongue (James 1:26) means controlling what you say, not how loud you say it. The joke compares it to talking loudly ('ALL CAPS'), which is a different action. 'ALL CAPS' also points at how his lines are written on screen.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The two blanks are 'orphans' (blank 1) and 'widows' (blank 2). A baker who places 'widows' first and 'orphans' second has named both groups correctly, but will be marked wrong on the order alone.
findings.question: When the two right words in a two-blank card could go in either order and keep the same meaning, should either order count as right, or should the card be reworded so that only one order makes sense?
